Newborn long-tailed macaques weigh approximately 320 grams [Wwb = approximately 320 grams], a neonatal mass that reflects the species' moderately precocial developmental pattern. This initial body size is consistent with typical values observed among cercopithecine primates of comparable adult dimensions. The gestation period required to bring a foetus to this birth mass extends to 165 days [tg = 165 days] when measured at the species' typical core body temperature of 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], a duration that aligns closely with gestational lengths reported for other members of the Macaca genus. During this uterine phase, organogenesis and rapid foetal growth proceed under tightly regulated thermal conditions, with the maternal thermoregulatory system maintaining the developing embryo at a stable internal environment. Field observations suggest that variation in maternal nutritional status can influence birth mass within a modest range, but the average value of 320 grams remains remarkably consistent across both wild and captive populations. This neonatal mass represents approximately five percent of the ultimate adult body weight, a ratio that is typical for macaque species and indicative of a life-history strategy that balances relatively large neonatal size against the energetic constraints of gestation within a moderately long pregnancy.

Weaning represents a critical nutritional transition in the development of juvenile long-tailed macaques, marking the cessation of lactation and the onset of dietary independence. The time since birth at which this transition typically occurs is 242 days [tx = 242 days] under the species' normal body temperature of 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], a timing that corresponds to the period when the infant's digestive system becomes capable of processing solid foods efficiently. At the point of weaning, the offspring have attained a wet weight of approximately 848 grams (848.4 grams) [Wwx = 848.4 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic growth achieved during the suckling phase. The age at weaning in this species is notably later than in some smaller-bodied primates but is comparatively early relative to great apes, fitting an intermediate position within the primate order. Following weaning, juveniles enter a prolonged sub-adult phase during which they continue to grow while learning essential foraging and social skills within the troop's complex hierarchical structure.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult long-tailed macaques is approximately 6393 grams [Wwi = approximately 6393 grams], representing the asymptotic body mass achieved at the completion of the growth trajectory. This adult mass is typical for a medium-sized macaque species and is associated with a pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males routinely exceeding females in both body mass and skeletal dimensions. The reproductive strategy of this species is characterized by a relatively low maximum reproductive rate, with females producing a single infant per birth event [N_R_i = single infant per birth event] and typically experiencing one birth each year [F_R_i = one birth each year]. This annual reproductive frequency, combined with the gestation length of 165 days, results in a slow life-history pace that is common among long-lived primates. The extended period of maternal investment, encompassing both gestation and lactation, is energetically costly and limits the potential for rapid population turnover. In captivity, well-nourished females may occasionally produce offspring at shorter intervals, but the one-year interbirth interval remains the norm across most established colonies.

Sexual maturation in long-tailed macaques occurs at different ages depending on the sex of the individual, a pattern of pubertal dimorphism observed across many primate species. Females typically reach puberty at 1238 days after birth [tp = 1238 days after birth] when maintained at a body temperature of 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C], corresponding to approximately three and a half years of age. Males, by contrast, attain sexual maturity considerably later, at 1544 days after birth [tp = 1544 days after birth] under the same thermal conditions, a delay of roughly 10.5 months relative to females at a temperature of 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C]. This sex-based difference in pubertal timing is thought to reflect the extended period required for males to achieve the larger body size necessary for successful competition in the dominance hierarchies that regulate access to receptive females. The onset of puberty in both sexes is accompanied by pronounced hormonal changes, including the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, which triggers gametogenesis and the development of secondary sexual characteristics. In wild populations, variation in food availability and social stress can modulate the precise timing of these maturational events.

The maximum lifespan documented for long-tailed macaques, measured under captive conditions where predation and disease are minimized, extends to approximately 39 years [am = approximately 39 years] at a body temperature of 37.6 °C [T = 37.6 °C]. This longevity places the species among the longer-lived members of the primate order relative to its body size, a characteristic that is consistent with a life-history strategy emphasizing extended somatic maintenance and delayed senescence. In wild populations, the average lifespan is considerably shorter due to extrinsic mortality factors including predation, intraspecific aggression, and resource limitation, but the physiological potential for extended survival remains encoded in the species' fundamental biology. The reproductive period spans a substantial portion of this lifespan, with females typically remaining reproductively active from puberty well into their third decade before experiencing reproductive senescence. The combination of prolonged gestation, extended lactation, late sexual maturation, and a long maximum life expectancy forms a coherent slow life-history syndrome that is typical of macaques. Comparative analyses with other cercopithecines suggest that this suite of life-history traits has been shaped by the species' evolutionary history in relatively stable tropical environments where delayed reproduction and extended parental investment enhance offspring survival and fitness.
